div.head: Bilateral craniotomy in a patient for concurrent aneurysm clipping and glioma resection: Anesthetic challenges
div.p: Dear Editor, Bilateral craniotomy (BC) for concurrent aneurysm clipping and glioma excision is rare. This report focuses on the anesthesia and neuromonitoring problems encountered during BC.
A 62-year-old hypertensive woman (ASA 2) presented with right lower limb weakness. Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging revealed a left parasagittal glioma with a midline shift [Figure 1a].

The MR angiogram unexpectedly showed a large anterior communicating artery (Acom) aneurysm. Angiography showed a wide-neck Acom aneurysm (12.5 × 6.3 × 6 mm) [Figure 1b] that filled from the right anterior cerebral artery (ACA). Aneurysm clipping (considering the wide neck) and glioma excision were planned in the same setting. Under balanced anesthesia (propofol target-controlled infusion (TCI), fentanyl (50 μg/h), cis-atracurium (2 μg/kg/min), and bilateral scalp block, a right pterional craniotomy was performed for aneurysm clipping. Because propofol TCI made the brain lax, further antiedema measures were avoided to prevent aneurysm rupture due to a sudden drop in intracranial pressure (ICP). A temporary clip was applied to the A1 segment of the right ACA under somatosensory evoked potential monitoring. The aneurysm was clipped successfully, after which the right pterional incision was closed. The patient was repositioned (supine with head flexed and rotated) for the left frontoparietal parasagittal craniotomy, and the glioma was resected. During the second craniotomy, mannitol (1.5 g/kg) was administered, and mild hyperventilation was instituted with propofol TCI. The patient was ventilated overnight in the intensive care unit. The trachea was extubated the next day, and the patient was neurologically intact.

The aneurysm must be secured first, either by clipping or coiling. [1] Although stent-assisted coiling can be performed for wide-neck aneurysms, the use of heparin and antiplatelet medications precludes immediate craniotomy. Additionally, anticoagulation can result in intratumoral bleeding in gliomas. [2] Monitoring the anesthetic depth can be challenging during BC. We placed the bispectral index (BIS) sensor on the contralateral forehead during the first craniotomy, but we were unable to monitor BIS during the second craniotomy. Alternative sites for placing the BIS sensor can be considered in these scenarios. [3] Because the cranial electrodes for transcranial motor evoked potential (tcMEP) monitoring are placed anteriorly, we were unable to monitor tcMEP during glioma resection. As a result, direct cortical MEP can be used to monitor the motor tracts. Good intraoperative analgesia is essential during BC, which we provided using a scalp block and fentanyl infusion. The aneurysmal transmural pressure is the difference between mean arterial pressure and ICP. Hence, a sudden rapid drop in ICP raises the risk of aneurysm rupture. [4] In contrast, a brain tumor with a mass effect necessitates lowering the ICP. Although mannitol can be administered slowly during aneurysm clipping, we avoided it to prevent a sudden drop in ICP. Furthermore, there is no consensus on whether mannitol should be administered in unruptured aneurysms without brain swelling. [5] Finally, considerable brain swelling can occur due to bilateral brain handling, which may necessitate postoperative elective ventilation.
